title: GST_112 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: The three fundamental components of culture identified in the course are:
questions.why: Why D is right: The course names exactly these three: technological (material culture), sociological (institutions and norms) and ideological (beliefs and values). Why the others are wrong: A substitutes 'economic' for sociological; the economy is never listed as a component of culture · B 'material' is only the gloss on technological, and 'associational' is one of the two forms of society, not a component of culture · C 'communal' is the other form of society, borrowed from the communal/associational pair

questions.q: Which theory views society as an organism in which each component plays a crucial role?
questions.why: Why A is right: This is the course's exact wording: functionalism sees society as an organism where each component plays a crucial role. Why the others are wrong: B Marx is the other named theory in Week 1, but he prescribes collective ownership of the means of production, he does not describe society as an organism · C a Week 12 theory of deviance, which explains deviance as a consequence of material inequality · D a Week 12 theory of deviance, which explains deviance as the result of a deviant label being applied to a person

questions.q: Communal and associational societies are said to differ in three named respects. Which three?
options: division of labour, religion and language
division of labour, social interactions and traditions
population size, settlement pattern and occupation
questions.why: Why B is right: These are the three criteria the course uses to separate the communal form of society from the associational form. Why the others are wrong: A culture and language are the Week 2 factors for identifying ethnic groups, not the criteria separating forms of society · C the rural-versus-urban feel that students substitute for the three stated criteria · D these are institutions, and so belong under the sociological component of culture

questions.q: In a Nigerian market town, the stalls and lock-up shops, the rules governing who may trade in which section, and the shrine of the deity the traders honour correspond respectively to which components of culture?
questions.why: Why B is right: Buildings and crafts are material and therefore technological; trading rules are norms and therefore sociological; the deity is a belief and therefore ideological. Why the others are wrong: A swaps the first two: it treats a physical building as an institution and a trading rule as material culture · C swaps the last two: it makes the trading rules a belief system and the shrine an institution · D reverses the first and third, making the physical structures a matter of belief

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes nation-building from national integration?
options: Nation-building welds diverse groups into one political community; national integration mobilises resources for development and constructs a national identity.
Nation-building is the project of the colonial state; national integration is the project of the post-colonial state.
Nation-building mobilises resources for socio-economic and political development and constructs a national identity; national integration welds diverse groups into one political community.
Nation-building concerns cultural unity alone; national integration concerns economic development alone.
questions.why: Why C is right: The course defines nation-building as the whole project of resource mobilisation plus identity construction, and national integration specifically as the welding of diverse groups into one political community. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two definitions, which is the commonest error on this pair · B invents a chronological split the course never draws · D splits the two by subject matter, whereas the course separates them by scope ### Peoples of Nigeria and Pre-Colonial Intergroup Relations

questions.q: Which two factors does the course use to identify distinct groups in inter-group relations?
questions.why: Why C is right: Inter-group relations is defined as interaction between two or more distinct linguistic and cultural groups, so the two identifying factors are culture and language. Why the others are wrong: A religion is one of the four indicators of interaction, not one of the two identifying factors · B territory is never named as an identifying factor; it belongs to the conflict indicator · D ancestry belongs to traditions of origin, which is again an indicator rather than an identifying factor

questions.q: In the shared traditions of origin, the Kanuri are said to have descended from ___ and the Hausa from ___.
questions.why: Why D is right: The course states plainly that the Kanuri descended from Saif and the Hausa from Bayajidda, both traced to Baghdad. Why the others are wrong: A the classic swap of the two founders between the two peoples · B Kisra belongs to a separate legend, founding the Yoruba and Borgu Kingdoms, not the Kanuri · C puts the Yoruba and Borgu founder in place of the Hausa founder Bayajidda

questions.q: According to the Kisra legend, Kisra founded the Yoruba and Borgu Kingdoms and regarded which ruler as his brother?
questions.why: Why A is right: The course states that Kisra, believed to have originated in Baghdad, considered the Ooni of Ife his brother. Why the others are wrong: B the Mai appears in the Bayajidda legend, whose daughter Bayajidda married, not in the Kisra legend · C Benin enters through the Oranmiyan and Eweka connection with the Yoruba, a different tradition of origin · D a twentieth-century political title held by Ahmadu Bello, not a figure in any origin legend

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four indicators of pre-colonial intergroup relations?
questions.why: Why C is right: The four indicators are traditions of origin, conflict, trade and commerce, and religion. Marriage alliances are never listed as an indicator. Why the others are wrong: A this is the first of the four indicators, covering the Saif, Bayajidda and Kisra legends · B this is the second indicator, covering the Oyo-Nupe wars and the Kano-Katsina struggle over trade routes · D this is the third indicator, covering the Jukun-Tiv exchange and the trans-Saharan trade

questions.q: Under the trade and commerce indicator, the Jukun exchanged salt with the Tiv in return for:
questions.why: Why B is right: The course's example is that the Jukun exchanged salt for firewood from the Tiv. Why the others are wrong: A shea butter belongs to the Nupe, who exchanged it with the Yoruba · C potash is also on the Nupe list exchanged with the Yoruba, alongside bangles and brasswork · D another item on the Nupe-Yoruba exchange list, not the Jukun-Tiv one

questions.q: Which geo-political zone does the course describe as the most ethnically diverse?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course attaches this description to the North Central zone, listing Borgu, Nupe, Igala and Tiv among its peoples. Why the others are wrong: A the zone of the Edo, Itsekiri, Ijaw and Efik, noted for democratic systems and influential kingdoms, not for being the most diverse · B the Kanuri and Jukun zone, noted for unique socio-political systems · D the Igbo zone, noted for the democratic age-grade system

questions.q: Territorial fighting between the Igala and the Nsukka Igbo eventually forged political ties, and the course notes that the Illah speak Igbo while their masquerades speak Igala. Under which indicator does the course place this example?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course lists the Igala-Nsukka Igbo fighting and the Illah masquerades as an illustration that war itself produced lasting political and cultural ties, so the example sits under conflict. Why the others are wrong: A masquerades do appear under religion, but there the shared practice itself is the point; here the tie was forged by war · B that indicator covers exchanges of goods such as salt for firewood, not war-born political ties · D that indicator covers descent legends such as Saif, Bayajidda and Kisra, not the outcome of fighting ### The Slave Trade, Legitimate Trade and Company Rule

questions.q: Phillip Curtin described the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade as the largest intercontinental migration in western history, spanning a period of:
questions.why: Why D is right: Curtin's phrase in the course is 'spanning a period of 300 years in which the Africans in mass numbers crossed the Atlantic'. Why the others are wrong: A 200 years is how long Portugal is said to have dominated world trade, a different figure entirely · B a round number students supply from general knowledge; the course says 300 · C too short, and matched to no figure anywhere in the course

questions.q: Paul Lovejoy notes that how many Africans died in transit during the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade?
questions.why: Why B is right: The course attributes the figure of over 7 million dying in transit specifically to Paul Lovejoy. Why the others are wrong: A 15 million is the estimate for those who reached the Americas alive, not those who died · C 3 million is the civil war death toll of Week 5, not a slave trade figure · D a plausible near-miss that appears nowhere in the course

questions.q: The space allotted to each slave on the crossing is given by the course as:
questions.why: Why D is right: This is the exact measurement stated, and it is why a ship carried between 451 and 600 slaves. Why the others are wrong: A doubles the width; the course's figure is one foot · B shortens the length and deepens the height, reversing the 6 and the 4 · C again transposes the 6 and the 4 from the stated measurement

questions.q: In which century were the British the biggest slave traders, their ships carrying more than half of the total slaves taken from Africa?
questions.why: Why D is right: The course's sequence runs Portuguese before 1600, Dutch in the 17th century, British in the 18th, and New World settlers in the 19th. Why the others are wrong: A this is when the Dutch joined the Portuguese as leading slave-trading nations · B before 1600 the Portuguese were the chief slave traders in West Africa · C by then European nations were no longer active and Europeans settled in the New World organised the trade

questions.q: As the slave population in the New World swelled and became capable of rebellion, an uprising broke out in Puerto Rico in:
questions.why: Why D is right: The course gives 1527 as the year of the Puerto Rico uprising, the consequence of a swelling slave population. Why the others are wrong: A the date associated with Columbus reaching the Americas, not with any uprising · B the boundary year before which the Portuguese were the chief slave traders · C the year Britain began seizing slave ships and repatriating captives to Sierra Leone

questions.q: The Asiento was:
options: the papal division of the Old World, ceding Africa to Portugal and the Americas to Spain
the British system of licensing chartered trading companies on the Niger
the Spanish system granting the right to trade in slaves in the New World
the Portuguese monopoly over the slave ports of the Bight of Benin
questions.why: Why C is right: The course defines the Asiento as the Spanish system granting that right, and notes it later became transferable to other Europeans. Why the others are wrong: A that is the separate papal partition, which the course records but never calls the Asiento · B chartered licensing is the Royal Niger Company story of 1886, three centuries later · D the Bight of Benin appears as the last centre of the slave trade by 1840, not as a Portuguese licence

questions.q: In 1833 a bill to abolish slavery was sponsored in the British Parliament by:
questions.why: Why D is right: Buxton, a British parliamentarian, sponsored the 1833 bill and argued that for the slave trade to stop it must stop from Africa. Why the others are wrong: A Laird led the 1857 Niger expedition and formed the Central African Company; he was a merchant, not a parliamentarian · B Beecroft was appointed in 1849 for control and supervision, sixteen years after the bill · C Chamberlain became Colonial Secretary in 1895 and weakened the Royal Niger Company

questions.q: A Liverpool merchant in the 1840s argues that Britain gains more by keeping Africans in Africa than by shipping them out. According to the course, what was the economic reasoning behind abolition that he is expressing?
options: Africans should stay in Africa to grow cash crops and to buy European finished goods
African labour was needed for the gold and silver mines newly opened in the interior
The cost of the Atlantic crossing had risen beyond what planters could afford to pay
Missionary societies wanted converts kept within reach of West African stations
questions.why: Why A is right: The course gives exactly this motive: rapid economic and technological development in the metropole removed the need for slave labour, so Europe wanted Africans in Africa growing cash crops for its industries and forming a ready market for its finished goods. Why the others are wrong: B gold and silver mines were a New World destination for slaves, not an African industry · C shipping costs are never given as a cause; the course's argument is about raw materials and markets · D abolition sentiment did include a movement in Britain, the United States and parts of Europe, but the course's economic motive is cash crops and markets

questions.q: Which scholar argued that it was mainly because the development of productive forces stagnated at a certain stage in African history that the colonisers were able to subordinate the continent?
questions.why: Why D is right: The quotation about stagnated productive forces is attributed to Claude Ake. Why the others are wrong: A Rodney shares Soyinka's view that underdevelopment came from the twin evils of slavery and colonialism · B Soyinka is the author of the 'twin evils of slavery and colonialism' formulation · C Alcott is cited on the forced removal of millions, including a large percentage of skilled tradesmen and women

questions.q: The appointment of Beecroft in 1849 for control and supervision is described in the course as:
options: the beginning of Britain's direct influence in Nigeria
the establishment of the Oil River Protectorate
the start of the legitimate trade in palm oil
questions.why: Why B is right: The course marks 1849 as the point at which British influence in Nigeria became direct. Why the others are wrong: A the annexation is dated 1861, twelve years later · C the protectorate dates from 1884, after Consul Hewett's treaty-making tour · D legitimate trade rose after the 1851 bombardment of Lagos, when more ships came to buy produce

questions.q: In which year was the National African Company granted a Royal Charter, becoming the Royal Niger Company?
questions.why: Why D is right: 1886 is the year of the Royal Charter, and the slides' own quiz gives this answer. Why the others are wrong: A 1881 is the year the company applied for a charter and was refused on grounds of lack of capacity · B in 1882 it raised its capital to one million pounds, but French firms still made a charter impossible · C by 1887 the chartered company already controlled all the territories in the basin of the Niger

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the seven districts of the Oil River Protectorate?
questions.why: Why B is right: Onitsha was one of the three Delta trading ports established by Macgregor Laird's 1857 expedition, alongside Ado and Gbebe. The seven districts were Bonny, Forcados, Old Calabar, New Calabar, Benin, Brass and Opobo. Why the others are wrong: A Bonny is the first of the seven districts listed · C Opobo is the seventh of the districts listed · D Forcados is the second of the districts listed ### Constitutional Development and the Quest for Independence

questions.q: The Nigerian Council set up by Lord Lugard in 1914 was made up of:
questions.why: Why B is right: The course gives 36 members with six unofficial members, and says the Council performed only advisory functions. Why the others are wrong: A 45 is the size of both the Clifford and the Richards legislative councils, not the 1914 Council · C the six were unofficial members, not elected ones; election did not arrive until Clifford in 1922 · D inflates the total by ten; the figure to memorise is 36

questions.q: The legislative council under the Clifford Constitution of 1922 had a total of 45 members made up of:
options: 26 official members who were Europeans, 15 nominated members and 4 elected Nigerians
28 Nigerians of whom 4 were elected, the rest being officials and nominees
26 nominated members, 15 official members who were Europeans and 4 elected Nigerians
15 official members who were Europeans, 26 nominated members and 4 elected Nigerians
questions.why: Why A is right: This is the exact composition given for Clifford's council of 45. Why the others are wrong: B 28 Nigerians in a council of 45 is the Richards composition of 1947, not Clifford's · C swaps the official and nominated figures, which are 26 and 15 respectively · D again reverses 26 and 15, understating the European official bloc

questions.q: Under the Clifford Constitution the four elected seats were allocated as:
options: three to Lagos and one to Ibadan
three to Lagos and one to Calabar
two to Lagos and two to Calabar
three to Calabar and one to Lagos
questions.why: Why B is right: Clifford's four elected Nigerians were three from Lagos and one from Calabar. Why the others are wrong: A Ibadan is where the Action Group was formed in 1951; it had no elected seat under Clifford · C splits the seats evenly, losing the three-to-one weighting in favour of Lagos · D reverses the two towns, the commonest slip on this item

questions.q: Clifford divided Nigeria politically into three units. Which three?
options: Lagos Colony, the Western Region and the Northern Region
Lagos Colony, the Oil River Protectorate and the Northern Provinces
Lagos Colony, the Eastern Provinces and the Western Provinces
Lagos Colony, the Southern Provinces and the Northern Provinces
questions.why: Why D is right: These are the three units of the 1922 arrangement, with Lagos and the South under legislative-council law and the North under proclamation. Why the others are wrong: A regions did not exist until Richards introduced regionalism in 1947 · B the Oil River Protectorate had already been renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate in 1893 · C splits the South in two, which Clifford did not do

questions.q: Which Governor abolished the office of the Lieutenant Governor, abolished the provincial court, and introduced the doctrine of separation of power?
questions.why: Why A is right: Cameron, Governor from 1930, is credited with all three of these measures in the interlude before Richards. Why the others are wrong: B Thompson took over in 1926 with no concessions to his credit · C Bourdillon prepared the ground for a new constitution and appealed to northern leaders to join the legislative council · D Richards authored the 1947 constitution and introduced regionalism

questions.q: A constitution provides a regional House of Assembly in each of the three regions, keeps one central legislative council of 45 in which 28 members are Nigerians and 4 of those are elected, and makes the legislature bicameral in the north only. Which constitution is described?
questions.why: Why C is right: Regionalism, the 28 Nigerians among 45, and bicameralism confined to the north are the defining marks of the Richards Constitution. Why the others are wrong: A Clifford's council also had 45 members, but only 4 Nigerians in all and no regions of any kind · B Macpherson made the two chambers apply in the Western and Northern Regions and renamed the council the House of Representatives with 136 members · D Lyttleton introduced federalism and regionalised the judiciary; it did not create the regional Houses of Assembly

questions.q: Under the Macpherson Constitution the Legislative Council was renamed the House of Representatives and made supreme, with how many members?
questions.why: Why B is right: The Macpherson House of Representatives had 136 members and was made supreme. Why the others are wrong: A 45 is the size of the Clifford council and of the Richards council, not of Macpherson's House · C 36 is the size of Lugard's 1914 Nigerian Council · D a plausible round figure that matches nothing in the course

questions.q: Which statement about Sir Oliver Lyttleton is correct?
options: He was a Colonial Secretary rather than a Governor of Nigeria, and the constitution bearing his name introduced federalism.
He was Governor of Nigeria from 1948, and the constitution bearing his name introduced regionalism.
He was a Colonial Secretary, and the constitution bearing his name first introduced the elective principle.
He was Governor of Nigeria, and the constitution bearing his name removed Lagos from the Western Region.
questions.why: Why A is right: Lyttleton is the only one of the four constitution-makers who was a Colonial Secretary and not a governor, and his 1954 constitution introduced the federal system. Why the others are wrong: B 1948 is when Macpherson became Governor, and regionalism belongs to Richards in 1947 · C the elective principle came with Clifford in 1922, over thirty years earlier · D removing Lagos from the Western Region was Macpherson's act in 1951; Lyttleton then made it a Federal Capital Territory

questions.q: Under a new constitutional arrangement the judiciary is regionalised, Lagos is made a Federal Capital Territory, ministers control the departments in their ministries, and revenue allocation is based on derivation. Which constitution is described?
questions.why: Why B is right: These are the four stated significances of the Lyttleton Constitution. Why the others are wrong: A Macpherson removed Lagos from the Western Region and made it an independent area, but it was Lyttleton who made it the Federal Capital Territory, and Macpherson's ministers had no portfolios · C Richards introduced regionalism but left the Executive Council single and central, with no regionalised judiciary · D Clifford made Lagos Colony a separate unit; there was no derivation formula and no Nigerian ministers at all

questions.q: The Nigerian National Democratic Party was founded in 1923 by ___ and published the newspaper ___.
options: Herbert Macaulay; the West African Pilot
Herbert Macaulay; the Lagos Daily News
Nnamdi Azikiwe; the Lagos Daily News
questions.why: Why B is right: Macaulay founded the NNDP in 1923 and it founded the Lagos Daily News; the party won all three Lagos seats in 1923, 1928 and 1933. Why the others are wrong: A the West African Pilot was introduced and published by the NCNC, not the NNDP · C Azikiwe was the NCNC's first General Secretary; he did not found the NNDP · D Ikoli was a leader of the Nigerian Youth Movement, and the Daily Service was the NYM's newspaper

questions.q: When the NCNC was formed, its first president and its first General Secretary were, respectively:
questions.why: Why B is right: Macaulay was the first president and Azikiwe the first General Secretary; Azikiwe became President only after Macaulay died. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two offices, the most frequent error on the NCNC · C Ikoli was a Nigerian Youth Movement leader and held no NCNC office · D Awolowo's party was the Action Group, formed in Ibadan in 1951

questions.q: The Northern People's Congress, a conservative party established in 1951, emerged from which cultural organisation?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course states that the NPC emerged from the cultural organisation Jamiyya Mutanen Arewa. Why the others are wrong: A Egbe Omo Oduduwa, formed in 1945, was the cultural ancestor of the Action Group, not the NPC · B the Lagos Youth Movement became the Nigerian Youth Movement in 1935 · D the Zikist movement was the radical youth body inspired by Azikiwe ### Independence, the First Republic and the Civil War

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three questions the course identifies as the national question after 1960?
options: How do we develop a meaningful national identity?
Which region should produce the Head of State?
questions.why: Why D is right: The three questions are: What is Nigeria? Who are Nigerians? How do we develop a meaningful national identity? The question of which region holds power is a symptom the course discusses, not one of the three. Why the others are wrong: A this is the first of the three questions · B this is the second of the three questions · C this is the third of the three questions

questions.q: Efforts to bring Nigerians closer politically, economically and culturally failed because of five named political vices. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.why: Why A is right: The five named vices are official corruption, rigged elections, ethnic baiting, bullying and thuggery. Military insubordination belongs to the separate discussion of coups. Why the others are wrong: B this is the third of the five named vices · C this is the second of the five named vices · D this is the fifth of the five named vices

questions.q: The First National Development Plan ran in which years and focused on which three sectors?
questions.why: Why A is right: The FNDP of 1962 to 1968 focused on agriculture, industry and education, and the 1966 coup ended development planning. Why the others are wrong: B 1960 to 1966 is the period over which the course gives the shifting GNP shares, not the span of the Plan · C oil is not one of the three sectors; agriculture is, and agriculture's GNP share fell over the period · D health replaces industry, whose GNP share rose from 3.6 to 6.2 per cent over the period

questions.q: A regional development corporation of the First Republic builds its investment programme around cocoa and timber. Which region does it belong to?
questions.why: Why C is right: The comparative advantages given are cocoa and timber in the West, palm oil in the East, and groundnut in the North. Why the others are wrong: A the East's comparative advantage was palm oil · B the North's comparative advantage was groundnut · D the Mid-West was created as a region during the First Republic crises and had no development corporation on the course's list of three

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the five majors who led the coup of 15 January 1966?
questions.why: Why D is right: The five majors were Nzeogwu, Ifeajuna, Okafor, Anuforo and Ademoyega. Brigadier S. A. Ademulegun, Commandant of the First Brigade, was killed in that coup, not a plotter. Why the others are wrong: A Ifeajuna is the second of the five majors named · B Anuforo is the fourth of the five majors named · C Ademoyega is the fifth of the five majors named

questions.q: Which decree, listed among Ironsi's gaffes, did Gowon announce the repeal of immediately on becoming Head of State?
questions.why: Why C is right: Decree No. 34, the Unification Decree, is the fourth of Ironsi's four gaffes, and Gowon repealed it at once. Why the others are wrong: A Decree 100 of 1993 established the National Orientation Agency, twenty-seven years later · B a plausible near-miss on the number; the Unification Decree is 34 · D transposes the digits of Decree No. 34

questions.q: Ojukwu declared the independence of the Eastern Region on:
questions.why: Why B is right: The declaration of 30 May 1967 followed the failure of negotiations including the Aburi Accord, and resulted in war. Why the others are wrong: A 29 July 1966 is the date of the countercoup in which Ironsi was killed and Gowon became Head of State · C 15 January 1966 is the date of the first coup led by the five majors · D 12 January 1970 is the date Effiong surrendered to Gowon in Lagos, ending the war

questions.q: Of the twelve states created in 1967, how many were carved out of the Eastern Region, and how many of those were predominantly Igbo?
options: Three states, of which two were predominantly Igbo
Four states, of which one was predominantly Igbo
Three states, of which one was predominantly Igbo
Two states, of which one was predominantly Igbo
questions.why: Why C is right: The course states that three states were carved out of the Eastern region and only one was predominantly Igbo, the design being to isolate the Igbos. Why the others are wrong: A doubles the Igbo-majority count and so destroys the point about isolation · B four states from the East would leave only eight for the rest of the country · D understates the split of the East, which was three ways

questions.q: Which of the following did NOT formally recognise Biafra in 1968?
questions.why: Why D is right: The four OAU member states that formally recognised Biafra in 1968 were Tanzania, Gabon, Ivory Coast and Zambia. France provided supplies and logistics but is not on the recognition list. Why the others are wrong: A Tanzania is the first of the four recognising states · B Gabon is the second of the four recognising states · C Zambia is the fourth of the four recognising states

questions.q: The civil war ended when Effiong surrendered to Gowon in Lagos on:
questions.why: Why A is right: By January 1970 Biafra had been overrun; Ojukwu fled to Ivory Coast and Effiong surrendered in Lagos on 12 January 1970. Why the others are wrong: B 15 January is the date of the 1966 coup, borrowed here into the wrong year · C January 1968 is the date of the currency change used to squeeze Biafra, not of the surrender · D 30 May is the date of Ojukwu's 1967 declaration, three years earlier ### The Military in Nigerian Politics

questions.q: The first military coup in Africa occurred in:
questions.why: Why A is right: The course opens the topic by stating that the first military coup in Africa occurred in Egypt in 1952. Why the others are wrong: B 1966 is Nigeria's first coup, not Africa's · C attaches Nigeria's year to the right country · D attaches the right year to the wrong country

questions.q: A Head of State who had promised at the end of the civil war to terminate military rule by 1 October 1976 suddenly announced a postponement in 1974, and was removed the following year in a bloodless coup. Who was removed, who led the plot, and who became Head of State?
options: Gowon was removed, Murtala Muhammed led the plot, and Colonel Joseph Nanven Garba became Head of State
Ironsi was removed, Colonel Joseph Nanven Garba led the plot, and Gowon became Head of State
Gowon was removed, Colonel Joseph Nanven Garba led the plot, and Murtala Muhammed became Head of State
Gowon was removed, Buka Suka Dimka led the plot, and Obasanjo became Head of State
questions.why: Why C is right: This is the sequence of 29 July 1975: Garba led the plotters, the coup was bloodless, and Murtala Muhammed took power with Obasanjo as deputy. Why the others are wrong: A reverses plotter and beneficiary; Garba led but did not rule · B describes the 1966 countercoup, which was led by northern officers, not by Garba · D Dimka's coup was in 1976, it failed, and Obasanjo took office only after Murtala's assassination

questions.q: The 1976 coup attempt of Lieutenant-Colonel Buka Suka Dimka is characterised in the course as:
options: a successful bloodless coup that installed Obasanjo as Head of State
a failed coup in which Murtala Muhammed was assassinated and Obasanjo assumed office
a failed coup in which Gowon was assassinated and Murtala Muhammed assumed office
a successful coup that overthrew Shagari for being inept and corrupt
questions.why: Why B is right: Dimka assassinated Murtala Muhammed but the coup failed for want of support from senior officers, and Lieutenant-General Obasanjo assumed office as Head of State. Why the others are wrong: A the bloodless coup was Garba's in 1975; Dimka's was bloody and unsuccessful · C Gowon was removed alive in 1975 and was not assassinated at all · D that is Buhari's coup of 1983, seven years later

questions.q: After the failed coup of Major Gideon Orkar, how many men were arrested, convicted and summarily executed, and how long did it take to put the coup down?
options: 42 men; the coup was put down within 10 hours
42 men; the coup was put down within 10 days
24 men; the coup was put down within 10 hours
42 men; the coup was put down within 3 days
questions.why: Why A is right: The course gives a total of 42 men, military personnel and civilians, executed in July 1990, and says the declaration was quashed within 10 hours. Why the others are wrong: B gets the number right but stretches ten hours into ten days · C transposes the digits of 42 · D substitutes the three years of Idiagbon's house arrest for the ten hours

questions.q: Abacha's coup of 17 November 1993 overthrew:
options: the military government of Ibrahim Babangida
the civilian government of Shehu Shagari
the military government of Muhammadu Buhari
the interim government of Ernest Shonekan
questions.why: Why D is right: Following the annulment of June 12, Babangida handed over to an interim government under Shonekan, and Abacha struck just three months later, citing its stagnant nature and its inability to manage the democratic process. Why the others are wrong: A Babangida had already stepped aside and handed over to the interim government before Abacha's coup · B Shagari was overthrown by Buhari in 1983 · C Buhari was overthrown by Babangida in 1985 ### Nigeria's Modern Economic Realities

questions.q: According to the 2006 census, Nigeria's population stood at:
questions.why: Why B is right: The course gives the 2006 census figure as 140,431,790. Why the others are wrong: A reduces the leading figure by twenty million; the census total begins with 140 · C transposes the middle digits of the census figure · D 180 million is the 2015 estimate, not the 2006 census

questions.q: The course describes Nigeria as the sixth most populated nation in the world, after which five countries?
options: China, India, the USA, Pakistan and Brazil
China, India, the USA, Indonesia and Brazil
China, India, the USA, Indonesia and Russia
India, China, the USA, Bangladesh and Brazil
questions.why: Why B is right: These are the five countries the course lists ahead of Nigeria. Why the others are wrong: A substitutes Pakistan for Indonesia, which is fourth on the course's list · C substitutes Russia for Brazil, which is fifth on the course's list · D substitutes Bangladesh for Indonesia

questions.q: Following the return to democracy in 1999, the course states that GDP grew from:
questions.why: Why B is right: 0.58 to 6.59 per cent is the growth attributed to the return to democracy in 1999. Why the others are wrong: A 1.89 to 4.89 per cent is the GDP movement between 1960 and 1965, before the coups · C mixes the 1999 starting point with the 1965 end point · D mixes the 1960 starting point with the 1999 end point

questions.q: Under President Olusegun Obasanjo, Nigeria obtained debt relief of ___ and foreign reserves rose above ___.
questions.why: Why A is right: The course gives debt relief of $20 billion and foreign reserves jumping above $64 billion under Obasanjo. Why the others are wrong: B $34 billion is the level to which reserves had dropped by 2015, not the debt relief · C puts the 2015 reserve level in place of the $64 billion peak · D reverses the two figures, making the debt relief larger than the reserves

questions.q: After the United States announced a reduced purchase of Nigerian crude in 2014, which country replaced it as Nigeria's major buyer?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course states that India replaced the US as the major buyer of Nigerian crude after the shale-driven announcement of 2014. Why the others are wrong: A China appears in the course as a country that showed support for Biafra with no serious material support, and as the world's most populous nation, not as the replacement buyer · B Brazil appears as a slave-trade destination and as the fifth most populous country, not as a crude buyer · D Malaysia appears only in the comparison that Nigeria was tipped to overtake it as a top-20 economy by 1980

questions.q: A federal official argues that Nigeria must stop depending on a single commodity for revenue and should instead build industrial parks, boost local refining and invest in tourism. Which of the course's ten named solutions is he advocating?
options: economic tutelage from a metropolitan state
questions.why: Why A is right: Economic diversification is the first of the ten solutions, and the course's conclusion is that Nigeria's problems will worsen without diversifying away from crude oil. Why the others are wrong: B revenue diversification is one of the six austerity measures of Week 9, aimed at government income rather than at the structure of the economy · C this is also on the list of ten solutions, but it means taking economic guidance from an advanced state, not restructuring output · D another Week 9 austerity measure, concerned with closing the budget deficit ### Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law

questions.q: Human rights are contained in which chapter and which sections of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.why: Why D is right: The course states that human rights are contained in Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, Sections 33 to 46. Why the others are wrong: A Chapter III of the Constitution deals with citizenship, not with rights · B Section 24 sets out the duties of the citizen; it is not the opening of the rights chapter · C gets the sections right but places them in the wrong chapter

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five common human rights abuses in Nigeria named in the course?
questions.why: Why C is right: The five named abuses are extra-judicial killing, rape, freedom of expression, child marriage and domestic violence. Human trafficking appears in Week 12 as the tenth effect of kidnapping. Why the others are wrong: A this is the fourth of the five named abuses, carrying the 43 per cent and 16 per cent figures · B this is the first of the five named abuses, the one linked to the EndSARS protests · D this is the fifth of the five named abuses, the one addressed by the VAPP Act

questions.q: The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act was signed into law in which year, and under which of the five abuses does the course treat it?
questions.why: Why A is right: The VAPP Act was signed into law in 2015 and is discussed under domestic violence, criminalising various forms of abuse and providing for reporting and prosecution. Why the others are wrong: B gets the year right but attaches the Act to the wrong abuse; child marriage is discussed under international law and the Aliogo figures · C 2009 is the year of the Rules that the course says still have shortcomings and inhibitions · D 1999 is the year of the Constitution whose Chapter IV holds the rights

questions.q: According to Aliogo (2023), what proportion of girls in Nigeria are married before their 18th birthday and before the age of 15 respectively?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course gives 43 per cent married before the 18th birthday and 16 per cent before the age of 15. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two figures, which would make marriage before 15 commoner than marriage before 18 · B keeps the first figure but inflates the second · D transposes the digits of 43 in the first figure

questions.q: How many cases of rights violations did the National Human Rights Commission receive in 2021?
questions.why: Why C is right: The NHRC received 1,701,519 cases of rights violations in 2021, higher than the previous year. Why the others are wrong: A 1,287,280 is the number of complaints the Commission received in 2020 · B 367,000 is the figure for women and gender-related issues in Nigeria in 2021 · D a near-miss on the leading digits of the 2021 figure

questions.q: On the Democracy Index, Nigeria is classified as:
questions.why: Why D is right: The course states that Nigeria is classified as a hybrid state because of its challenges in meeting the criteria of a full democracy. Why the others are wrong: A the neighbouring Democracy Index category that students most often substitute for hybrid state · B the category the course explicitly says Nigeria fails to meet the criteria for · C the bottom Democracy Index category, which the course does not apply to Nigeria

questions.q: A state government orders a television station off air after it broadcasts a report on political corruption. Which body does the course identify as the instrument through which government controls much of the electronic media?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course states that the government controlled much of the electronic media through the NBC, which is responsible for monitoring and regulating broadcast media and was used to clamp down on television and radio stations. Why the others are wrong: A the NOA is a Week 9 reorientation body created to build public support for government policies, not a broadcast regulator · B the NHRC receives complaints of rights violations; it does not license or regulate broadcasters · D a plausible-sounding regulator that the course never names ### Citizenship and Civic Responsibilities

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT make a person a citizen of Nigeria by birth?
options: being born within Nigeria to two foreign parents
any one of the grandparents being a Nigerian
questions.why: Why A is right: The three conditions for citizenship by birth are that both parents are Nigerians, that either parent is a Nigerian, or that any one of the grandparents is a Nigerian. Birth on Nigerian soil to foreign parents is not among them. Why the others are wrong: B this is the first of the three stated conditions · C this is the second of the three stated conditions · D this is the third of the three stated conditions

questions.q: A Ghanaian woman marries a Nigerian man and applies to become a Nigerian. Under the 1999 Constitution she acquires citizenship by which route?
questions.why: Why C is right: Citizenship by registration is open to a non-Nigerian woman married to a Nigerian, and to a person of full age born outside Nigeria whose grandparent is a Nigerian citizen. Why the others are wrong: A naturalisation under Section 27 is the route for a foreigner who has lived in Nigeria for a long time, not for a foreign wife · B citizenship by birth turns on parentage and grandparentage, and marriage cannot create it · D the President's role is to be satisfied of good character, intention to reside, and the Oath of Allegiance, not to grant citizenship as a separate route

questions.q: Musa became a Nigerian by naturalisation and, six years later, was convicted and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. What does the Constitution permit?
options: The President may deprive him of his Nigerian citizenship
He cannot be deprived, because a sentence must exceed seven years
He cannot be deprived, because he is now a citizen like any other
He automatically loses his citizenship on conviction
questions.why: Why A is right: A person who is not a Nigerian by birth may be deprived of citizenship if sentenced to imprisonment of not less than 3 years within a period of 7 years of becoming a citizen. Four years, six years after, falls inside both limits. Why the others are wrong: B confuses the seven-year window with the length of sentence; the sentence threshold is three years · C true only of a citizen by birth; a naturalised or registered citizen can be deprived · D the loss is not automatic; it is a power the President may exercise

questions.q: On which grounds may the President refuse to register a declaration renouncing Nigerian citizenship?
options: Where the person is not of full age, or where it is contrary to public policy
Where the person has unpaid tax liabilities, or where Nigeria is involved in a war
Where it was made when Nigeria is involved in a war, or where it is contrary to public policy
Where the person has not rendered national service, or where it is contrary to public policy
questions.why: Why C is right: The Constitution gives exactly these two grounds for refusing to register a renunciation. Why the others are wrong: A full age is a precondition of renouncing at all, not a ground on which the President refuses registration · B tax appears in Section 24 as a civic duty, never as a bar to renunciation · D national service is a civic responsibility, not a condition of renunciation

questions.q: The requirements for citizenship by naturalisation are stipulated in which section of the 1999 Constitution?
questions.why: Why A is right: The course states that naturalisation is governed by Section 27, after which a certificate of grant of citizenship by naturalisation is issued. Why the others are wrong: B Section 24 sets out the duties of every citizen, not the requirements for naturalisation · C Section 33 opens the human rights provisions of Chapter IV · D a near-miss within the citizenship chapter, but the course names 27

questions.q: The duties of every citizen are set out in which section of the 1999 Constitution, and the prescribed Oath of Allegiance is contained in which schedule?
questions.why: Why A is right: Section 24 lists the lettered duties of the citizen, and the Oath of Allegiance taken by an applicant for registration is contained in the Seventh Schedule. Why the others are wrong: B Section 27 governs naturalisation, not the duties of the citizen · C gets the section right but moves the Oath of Allegiance to the wrong schedule · D moves the duties into the opening citizenship section

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six civic responsibilities named in the course?
questions.why: Why D is right: The six civic responsibilities are obeying the law, protection of public property, payment of taxes, rendering national service, loyalty, and respect for others' rights. Voter registration drives appear in Week 10 as a form of youth political awakening. Why the others are wrong: A this is the second of the six civic responsibilities · B this is the fourth of the six civic responsibilities · C this is the third of the six civic responsibilities ### Reorientation Strategies

questions.q: The National Orientation Agency was established by which decree and in which year?
questions.why: Why B is right: The NOA, successor of the Directorate for Social Mobilisation, was established by Decree 100 of 1993. Why the others are wrong: A Decree No. 34 is Ironsi's Unification Decree, repealed by Gowon · C 1987 is the year MAMSER was launched, not the year of the NOA decree · D gets the year right but not the decree number

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six reorientation efforts named in the course?
questions.why: Why A is right: The six efforts are the NOA, Operation Feed the Nation, Austerity Measures, War Against Indiscipline, War Against Indiscipline and Corruption, and MAMSER. The Green Revolution is a programme under Operation Feed the Nation, dated 1980. Why the others are wrong: B Mass Mobilisation for Self-reliance, Social Justice and Economic Recovery is the sixth of the six efforts · C WAIC is listed as the fifth of the six efforts, distinct from the War Against Indiscipline · D austerity measures are the third of the six efforts

questions.q: Operation Feed the Nation was introduced by which head of state, and in which years did it run?
questions.why: Why B is right: The course dates Operation Feed the Nation to 1976 to 1980 and attributes it to the military government of General Olusegun Obasanjo. Why the others are wrong: A Buhari ran the War Against Indiscipline, which ended in September 1985 · C 1979 to 1983 is the span of the Shagari civilian government · D Babangida is associated with the Structural Adjustment Programme, not with Operation Feed the Nation

questions.q: Which of the programmes listed under Operation Feed the Nation is dated 1986 in the course?
options: the Directorate for Food, Roads and Rural Infrastructure
questions.why: Why C is right: DFRRI is given the date 1986, later than the rest of the list, but the course still places it under Operation Feed the Nation. Why the others are wrong: A the Green Revolution is dated 1980 · B the Rural Banking System is dated 1978, alongside the River Basin Development Programme · D the Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme is dated 1977

questions.q: The War Against Indiscipline was organised by which government, and when did the programme end?
options: the military dictatorship of Buhari; September 1983
the military dictatorship of Buhari; September 1985
the military government of Babangida; September 1985
the military government of Obasanjo; December 1985
questions.why: Why B is right: The course states that WAI was a mass mobilisation programme of Buhari's military dictatorship and that the programme ended in September 1985. Why the others are wrong: A 1983 is the year Buhari's coup brought him to power, not the year WAI ended · C Babangida took power in 1985 but WAI was Buhari's programme · D Obasanjo's reorientation programme was Operation Feed the Nation, which ended in 1980

questions.q: MAMSER was launched in 1987 following the recommendation of the Public Bureau headed by:
questions.why: Why A is right: The course names Samuel Cookey as the head of the Public Bureau whose recommendation produced MAMSER. Why the others are wrong: B Aminu Kano is named as one of the founders of the Northern People's Congress in 1951 · C Shonekan headed the interim government of 1993 that Abacha overthrew · D Garba led the plotters who removed Gowon in 1975

questions.q: A federal agency runs a Campaign Against Open Defecation, a nationwide sensitisation on the Freedom of Information Act, and a 'Change Begins With Me' campaign urging Nigerians to patronise made-in-Nigeria products. Which agency is described?
questions.why: Why D is right: All three are on the NOA's list of eight programmes, alongside its attitudinal reorientation work in schools and tertiary institutions. Why the others are wrong: A MAMSER's work was mobilisation for self-reliance, social justice and economic recovery, and it was phased out before these campaigns existed · B the NBC monitors and regulates broadcast media; it runs no public reorientation campaigns · C this is MAMSER under its other name, the body the NOA succeeded ### Pop Culture, Police Brutality and Youth Awakening

questions.q: The term 'popular culture' was coined in which period?
options: the period after the Second World War
questions.why: Why C is right: The course states that the term was coined in the mid-19th century, contrasting the cultural traditions of the people with the official culture of the state or governing classes. Why the others are wrong: A too late; this is closer to the period of the mass media innovations that followed the Second World War · B too early; the Industrial Revolution created the middle class the scholars trace popular culture to, but the term itself came later · D the post-war years brought the mass media innovations that changed popular culture, but the term already existed

questions.q: The First Wave of Nigerian popular music, dated 1950 to 1967, is described as deeply traditional and saw the evolution of which genres?
questions.why: Why A is right: These are the three genres the course attaches to the First Wave, whose external influences were Ghanaian Highlife, Caribbean calypso and Mambo. Why the others are wrong: B Fuji belongs to the Second Wave, and Waka and Afro Juju were introduced in the Third Wave of 1980 to 1990 · C Afrobeat and Fuji both became mainstream in the Second Wave of 1967 to 1980 · D Yo Pop is a Third Wave sound associated with Segun Adewale

questions.q: Fuji emerged as a fusion of which two genres?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course defines Fuji as a fusion of Apala and Ajisari, drawing major influences from Islam and appealing mostly to the lower class. Why the others are wrong: A Juju was the upper-class genre of Obey and Sunny Ade, and is not a parent of Fuji · B both are First Wave genres, but neither is a parent of Fuji · D Waka is a Third Wave sound associated with Salawa Abeni, later than Fuji's emergence

questions.q: A Nigerian musician records in Ajegunle, fuses his sound with reggae and R&B in a bid to reach an international audience, and complains that Nigerian music now sounds more American than Nigerian just as the foreign record labels are leaving. Which wave is described?
options: the Fourth Wave, 1992 to the present
questions.why: Why B is right: The Third Wave is the era of the Ajegunle sounds, the fusion with reggae, calypso, rap and R&B, the departure of the international labels, and the struggle for a Nigerian identity. Why the others are wrong: A the quest to sound American continued into the Fourth Wave, but that wave is marked by groups such as the Remedies and Plantashun Boiz and by the later return to local languages · C the Second Wave is the era of the Highlife revival, Fela's Afrobeat and the rise of Fuji, not of the international labels departing · D the First Wave was deeply traditional, its external influences being Ghanaian Highlife, calypso and Mambo

questions.q: The #EndSARS agitation first appeared as a hashtag on which platform and in which year?
questions.why: Why D is right: The protest began as a hashtag on Twitter in 2017 and metamorphosed into a crisis in October 2020. Why the others are wrong: A 2020 is when the hashtag metamorphosed into a crisis, three years after it first appeared · B the course specifies Twitter, which it says was especially deployed to achieve the protest's purpose · C two years too early; the course dates the hashtag to 2017

questions.q: On what date did the Nigerian Army open fire on protesters at the Lekki toll gate?
questions.why: Why C is right: The course dates the Lekki shooting to 20 October 2020, during the three weeks of protest in October 2020. Why the others are wrong: A 2017 is the year the hashtag first appeared on Twitter, not the year of the shooting · B right month and year, wrong day · D 25 February 2023 is one of the two election dates for which the movement generated new voter registrations

questions.q: The course gives the countrywide voter turnout in 2023, describing it as the lowest in Nigeria's six decades of independence, as:
questions.why: Why B is right: Turnout in 2023 was 29 per cent, which the course calls the lowest in six decades of independence. Why the others are wrong: A 40 per cent is the share of the newly registered young voters who registered as students · C 76 per cent is the share of newly registered voters who were young people · D 60 per cent is the share of Nigeria's population made up of youth

questions.q: Which scholar argues that the Nigerian Police have not been decolonised, since in the colonial period they existed for the suppression of revolts and 'brute force was the primary operating philosophy of the police'?
questions.why: Why A is right: This argument and this quotation are attributed to Moses Ochonu. Why the others are wrong: B Oyarinu is the other named scholar in this topic, who traces SARS to the failing economy, the depreciating naira, the civil war, SAP and poor leadership · C Ake is a Week 3 scholar on the stagnation of Africa's productive forces · D Rodney is a Week 3 scholar on the twin evils of slavery and colonialism ### Makers of Nigeria

questions.q: Which of the Makers of Nigeria protested British policies on water rates, land issues and the management of railway finances during the 1920s, and is tagged the father of Nigerian nationalism?
questions.why: Why A is right: Macaulay is the father of Nigerian nationalism, among the first generation of nationalists, and the protester of water rates, land issues and railway finances. Why the others are wrong: B Azikiwe worked to end British control as a journalist and politician and joined politics in 1944, a generation after these protests · C Awolowo's contribution was federalism and the premiership of the Western Region from 1954 · D Ransome-Kuti mobilised market women against colonial rule and is the 'Lioness of Lisabi'

questions.q: Nnamdi Azikiwe held which two offices in succession?
options: Last governor-general from 1960 to 1963, then first elected president from 1963 to 1966
First elected president from 1960 to 1963, then last governor-general from 1963 to 1966
Last governor-general from 1963 to 1966, then first elected president from 1966 to 1979
First premier of the Eastern Region, then first elected president from 1963 to 1966
questions.why: Why A is right: The course places Azikiwe as last governor-general 1960 to 1963 and then first elected president 1963 to 1966, during the First Republic. Why the others are wrong: B reverses the order of the two offices, which ran governor-general first · C shifts both terms forward; the presidency ended with the coup of January 1966 · D the premiership of a region belongs to Awolowo's profile, not Azikiwe's

questions.q: Obafemi Awolowo was the first premier of which region, and in which years?
questions.why: Why D is right: The course gives Awolowo as first premier of the Western Region from 1954 to 1960, the office created by the Lyttleton Constitution. Why the others are wrong: A 1951 is the year the Action Group was formed in Ibadan; the premiership came with Lyttleton in 1954 · B the Eastern Region's first regional government was formed by the NCNC · C extends the premiership to the first coup; the course ends it at independence

questions.q: The conference Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti organised in Abeokuta in 1953 to discuss women's welfare gave birth to which body?
options: the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies
questions.why: Why B is right: The course states that the 1953 Abeokuta conference gave birth to the FNWS. Why the others are wrong: A a plausible-sounding body that the course does not name in connection with the 1953 conference · C Egbe Omo Oduduwa was formed in 1945 by Awolowo, the Ooni and Ajasin · D the Zikist movement was the radical multi-ethnic youth body inspired by Azikiwe

questions.q: Wole Soyinka received the Nobel Prize for Literature in which year, and dedicated the award to whom?
questions.why: Why C is right: Soyinka was the first African to receive the Prize, in 1986, and dedicated it to the imprisoned Nelson Mandela while focusing attention on white rule in South Africa. Why the others are wrong: A gets the year right but substitutes a Ghanaian leader for the imprisoned South African · B 1994 is the year Soyinka fled Nigeria after being charged with treason · D 1967 is the year Soyinka, then 33, was imprisoned for 22 months for speaking out against the civil war

questions.q: A lawyer who began practising in Lagos in 1965, campaigned for human rights for 40 years, had his library set on fire, and pressed from his sick bed for the reopening of the Dele Giwa case before dying in 2009, is:
options: Gani Fawehinmi, known as 'the people's lawyer'
Gani Fawehinmi, known as 'the Lioness of Lisabi'
Nnamdi Azikiwe, known as 'the father of Nigerian nationalism'
Wole Soyinka, known as 'the people's lawyer'
questions.why: Why A is right: All of these details belong to Ganiyu Oyesola Fawehinmi, who took a great number of pro bono cases and so became known as the people's lawyer. Why the others are wrong: B the Lioness of Lisabi is the moniker of Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti · C that title belongs to Herbert Macaulay, and Azikiwe was a journalist and politician rather than a lawyer · D Soyinka was imprisoned and later exiled, but he is a writer and Nobel Laureate, not a lawyer ### Social Vices: Cultism, Kidnapping and Armed Robbery

questions.q: What is the subtle difference the course draws between crime and deviance?
options: Committing a crime violates social norms, while deviant behaviour violates social laws
Crime is punished only by fines, while deviance is punished by imprisonment
Committing a crime violates social laws, while deviant behaviour violates social norms and rules
Crime and deviance are used interchangeably and the course draws no difference between them
questions.why: Why C is right: The course notes that although the terms are used interchangeably, crime refers to actions prohibited by law with legal consequences, while deviance is the broader category of departure from societal norms or expectations. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two definitions, which is the commonest error on this pair · B the course says crime can result in fines or imprisonment, and gives no penalty at all for deviance as such · D the course expressly says they are used interchangeably but that subtle differences exist

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four theories of deviance?
questions.why: Why D is right: The four theories of deviance are Structural Functionalism, Social Strain Typology, Conflict Theory and Labelling Theory. Rational Choice Theory is one of the three theories of crime. Why the others are wrong: A this is the fourth of the four theories of deviance · B this is the third of the four theories of deviance · C this is the second of the four theories of deviance, and is easily confused with the Strain Theory on the crime list

questions.q: Which theory holds that deviant behaviour plays a constructive role in society, because it brings the different parts of the population together to agree on what is acceptable and what is not?
questions.why: Why D is right: This is the course's account of Structural Functionalism, the first of the four theories of deviance. Why the others are wrong: A Conflict Theory treats deviance as a consequence of material inequality, not as constructive · B Labelling Theory treats deviance as a consequence of a deviant label being applied to a person · C Social Learning Theory is a theory of crime, holding that criminal behaviour is acquired by observing and imitating others

questions.q: Campus cultism is traced to the early 1950s, when Wole Soyinka and six friends founded the Pirates Confraternity at:
questions.why: Why D is right: The course places the founding of the Pirates Confraternity at the University of Ibadan, as a social group whose founding beliefs were patriotic and philanthropic. Why the others are wrong: A a plausible substitution, but the course names Ibadan · B another plausible substitution not supported by the course · C Yaba Higher College appears in Week 4 as the institution the Nigerian Youth Movement wanted affiliated to a British university

questions.q: About how many secret cults does the course say are operating in Nigerian tertiary institutions today?
questions.why: Why B is right: The course says there are about forty-five secret cults operating in tertiary institutions, all with elaborate hierarchy, insignia and distinct attire. Why the others are wrong: A understates the count; the figure to memorise is forty-five · C a near-miss above the stated figure · D inflates the figure tenfold

questions.q: What jail term does the law stipulate for anyone found to be a member of a cult group, or who solicits members for an unlawful society?
questions.why: Why D is right: The course states a jail term of 21 years for membership of a cult group or solicitation of members for an unlawful society. Why the others are wrong: A 3 years is the sentence for allowing cult meetings in your residence or a structure belonging to you · B 7 years is the window within which a naturalised citizen's conviction can cost him citizenship, from Week 8 · C a plausible statutory term that the course never gives

questions.q: A landlord knowingly allows a cult group to hold its meetings in a building he owns. According to the course, what has he committed and what sentence does he face?
questions.why: Why B is right: Anyone who allows cult meetings in their residence, or in a structure that belongs to them, is regarded as committing a felony and will receive a 3-year sentence. Why the others are wrong: A 21 years is the penalty for membership or solicitation, not for hosting · C gets the sentence right but downgrades the offence; the course calls it a felony · D substitutes the seven-year citizenship window for the three-year sentence

questions.q: Which pair of figures does the course give for reported kidnap cases in Nigeria?
questions.why: Why D is right: These are the two kidnapping figures the course gives, for 2018 and 2022 respectively. Why the others are wrong: A inflates both kidnapping figures tenfold · B these are the armed robbery figures from prison records, which fall while kidnapping rises · C keeps the kidnapping figures but attaches the armed robbery years to them
